description: I am a solo software and game developer and creator of Xplore, a web platform that turns real space data into interactive 3D. Builds with React, Three.js, Unity and Blender, backed by Python and Django data pipelines, bringing a game developer’s eye to making complex science easy to explore.
summary:
NISAR SAR Observatory is an interactive web app that turns NASA-ISRO NISAR L-band radar into 3D change maps of five real events: Pine Island Glacier flow, the Venezuela earthquakes, the Hayli Gubbi eruption, the Mozambique floods and the Big Sur wildfires. Each event sits on a 3D globe, with a change map, a before/after slider, a timeline of repeat passes and 3D relief where height shows how strongly the ground changed.
The challenge asks how radar can reveal Earth’s changing surface. Radar sees through cloud, smoke and darkness, but a radar map only helps if people can trust it. So every map here is checked against an independent or official source: UC San Diego, ITS_LIVE, Sentinel-1C, Copernicus EMS and NIFC. Agreement and disagreement are drawn on the map. Results are strong for Venezuela (r = 0.96), Pine Island (r = 0.92) and Mozambique (89% inside the official flood map), and the two weaker results are shown openly.
This matters because responders, scientists and the public need maps they can act on. The app runs in any browser, including on phones, with no sign-in, and explains what changed, how the radar sees it and how far to trust it.
details:
Source Code (open-source snapshot of the NISAR files): https://github.com/spham11/nisar-sar-observatory

At a glance

NISAR L-band radar maps of five real events (ice flow, earthquakes, an eruption, floods, wildfires), each checked against a separate independent or official source. Strong agreement for Venezuela (r = 0.96, 97% of flagged area confirmed), Pine Island (r = 0.92) and Mozambique (89% of flags inside the official flood area). Weaker results are shown openly, not hidden. Live app: https://xplorespace.app/sar

What it does

NISAR SAR Observatory detects, monitors and visualizes Earth surface change at five real events using NISAR L-band radar, listed by science priority.

  • Pine Island Glacier flow: ice speed in metres per year, measured from how far the surface moved between two passes. Ice sheets and sea level are a core NISAR objective.
  • Venezuela earthquakes: ground displacement, showing how far the surface moved between two passes.
  • Hayli Gubbi eruption (Ethiopia): ground displacement around the volcano and the Erta Ale caldera, where the ground moved about 40 cm away from the satellite at the summit in the eruption pair.
  • Mozambique floods: new open water, found where radar backscatter drops as land turns into floodwater.
  • Big Sur wildfires: burn scars, found from backscatter change between passes.

Signals used: floods show up where HH backscatter drops, burn scars where HV falls and the HH/HV ratio rises, ground motion comes from interferometric phase (the shift between two passes), and ice speed comes from pixel-offset tracking.

Why these five places

The five events cover four kinds of change and the science priorities NISAR was built for: ice-sheet flow (tied to sea-level rise), earthquakes and a volcanic eruption (solid-earth hazards), floods (disaster response) and wildfire burn scars. Each event also has an independent or official reference to check against: ITS_LIVE, UC San Diego, Sentinel-1C, Copernicus emergency mapping and the US interagency fire perimeters.

How change is shown

  • Every event is a pin on a 3D globe. A guided flyby moves from event to event.
  • Three views per event: a Change map, a Before / After comparison with a draggable split, and a Timeline of repeat passes.
  • Change is drawn as 3D relief. Terrain height rises with change strength, so the places that changed most stand out at a glance.
  • The overview globe shows real day and night, with city lights on the night side.
  • Time windows resolve to the most recent pass, and the before image comes from the same track, direction and frame, so the comparison is like for like.
  • Works on any screen: on mobile the whole globe stays in view above a foldable event list, and the panels fit portrait and landscape, so the full app runs in a mobile browser with no install.

The scientific method, step by step

  1. Question: can a NISAR radar change map be trusted for real events, and where does it fall short?
  2. Hypothesis: maps made from NISAR L-band passes agree with independent or official measurements of the same event, and any disagreement can be located and explained.
  3. Method: five events chosen to cover four kinds of change. Each map is built from NISAR Level-2 products with a fixed, stated recipe (HH backscatter drop for floods, HV drop and HH/HV rise for burn scars, interferometric phase for ground motion, pixel-offset tracking for ice speed).
  4. Test: every result is compared against a reference that is independent of the map: a separate processing of the same pair (UC San Diego), other satellites (ITS_LIVE, Sentinel-1C, COSMO-SkyMed SG) or official maps (Copernicus EMS, NIFC). Agreement and disagreement are measured and drawn on the map (green: both agree, amber: radar only, red: reference only).
  5. Results: strong agreement for Venezuela (r = 0.96, 97% of the flagged area confirmed), Pine Island (r = 0.92) and Mozambique (89% of flagged ground inside the official flood area, 2.0% of other ground flagged). Partial agreement for Big Sur (62% of flagged ground inside the perimeters, 83% of the official area flagged with a 146 m edge tolerance) and Hayli Gubbi (peaks 0.3 km apart, same direction, Sentinel-1 at about 30% of the NISAR size with usable data on only 45% of the area).
  6. Conclusion: the hypothesis holds well for ground motion, ice flow and open water, and only partly for burn scars and the eruption. Those two are reported openly, with the reasons listed below, instead of being left out.
  7. Limits that shape the conclusion: one 12-day pair per event, PROVISIONAL data for three events, ITS_LIVE is a 2024 average (so Pine Island compares flow patterns, not the same days), fire perimeters are coarse, and the Copernicus flood map is dated 20 January while the radar pair ends earlier. The Venezuela reference is a separate processing of the same radar pair, so it checks the processing, not a second sensor.
  8. Reproducible: the pipeline starts from public ASF DAAC products, the product names, dates and methods are listed in the Data and methods panel, and the validation numbers on screen are read from the same data files, not typed in. A batch job checks for newer passes and refreshes the numbers.

How the result is checked

Each radar result is compared with independent or official data wherever that exists:

  • Venezuela earthquakes: checked against UC San Diego (TOPEX / GMTSAR), a separate processing of the same radar pair. Result shown on screen: correlation 0.96, typical difference 0.4 cm, 97% of the flagged area confirmed.
  • Pine Island Glacier: checked against the ITS_LIVE velocity record (other satellites). Result shown on screen: flow-pattern correlation 0.92. On the fastest ice (over 3,000 m/yr), NISAR is 4% below ITS_LIVE.
  • Mozambique floods: checked against Copernicus EMS EMSR857 (COSMO-SkyMed SG, X-band). Result shown on screen: 89% of flagged ground inside the official flood area, and 2.0% of other ground flagged.
  • Big Sur wildfires: checked against the NIFC interagency fire perimeters. Result shown on screen: 62% of flagged ground inside the perimeters and 57% of the official area flagged. With a 146 m tolerance for the coarse perimeter edges: 83% of the official area flagged, 62.5% of flagged ground inside, and 1.8% of ground far from any perimeter flagged.
  • Hayli Gubbi eruption: checked against a Sentinel-1C interferogram (ASF HyP3, 19 Nov to 1 Dec 2025). Result shown on screen: strongest motion 0.3 km apart, same direction. Sentinel-1 shows about 30% of the NISAR size and has usable data on only 45% of the area.

A validation card shows an agreement map (green: both agree, amber: radar only, red: reference only), an agreement bar in km² and a plain-language verdict. Places where radar and the official map disagree are shown openly, not hidden. Fire perimeters are coarse, so the Big Sur check also reports the result with a small tolerance around the perimeter edge. The caveats of each reference are written on the card. For example, ITS_LIVE is a 2024 average and the NISAR result is one 12-day pair, and the Copernicus flood map is from 20 January while the radar pair ends earlier.

Try it in 60 seconds

  1. Open https://xplorespace.app/sar and tap any event pin on the globe.
  2. Switch between Change map, Before / After (drag the split) and Timeline.
  3. Open the validation card: green is where radar and the reference agree, amber is radar only, red is reference only.
  4. Press the guided flyby for the full tour. No sign-in, no install, and it works on a phone.

Who benefits

  • Responders and mapping teams: flood and burn extents found through cloud and smoke, with a stated agreement figure instead of a guess.
  • Earthquake and volcano scientists: ground movement between passes, checked against independent processing.
  • Ice and sea-level researchers: Pine Island flow speed in metres per year, compared with ITS_LIVE.
  • Students, teachers and the public: 3D relief and plain-language verdicts that need no radar training.

What makes it different

  • Results are validated against official and independent maps, with the disagreement drawn on the map and written on the card.
  • Three different kinds of change (ground motion, water, burn) plus ice flow share one way of exploring them.
  • The 3D relief turns a radar image into something readable without radar training.
  • The whole story is explained inside the app: what changed, how the radar sees it, and how the result was checked.
  • Each event also explains why it happened, with the physical driver taken from published sources: strain on the Caribbean and South American plate boundary for Venezuela, a contracting dike at Erta Ale, weeks of intense rain overwhelming reservoirs in Mozambique, warm ocean water melting the ice shelf at Pine Island, and fire stripping canopy at Big Sur.
  • For the Mozambique flood, the page also shows roughly 47,300 people living inside the 1,257 km² of officially mapped flood area (Copernicus EMSR857). This is a modelled estimate from the WorldPop 2020 constrained 100 m population grid (University of Southampton, https://www.worldpop.org), not a count of people affected.
  • Polarization matters for what each map shows. Floods use the HH channel, where calm open water turns dark and flooded vegetation turns bright. Big Sur burn scars use the HV (cross-polarized) channel, which responds mainly to scattering inside the forest canopy and drops when fire strips leaves and branches.
  • A Data and methods panel lists the NISAR product, data maturity, dates, method, reference data and caveats for every event in one place.

What is next

  • More events as the NISAR archive grows: the batch job already checks for newer passes, so new passes extend the existing events and new events can be added the same way.
  • New kinds of change that L-band suits well: wetland and floodplain water, crop type and health, soil moisture, sea ice and coastal subsidence.
  • A repeat-pass timeline for every event, plus the same validation card, checked against an independent reference, for each new event type.
  • S-band data from the ISRO side of the mission, alongside L-band, to compare how the two wavelengths see the same change.

Honest limits (also written on the cards in the app)

  • NISAR L-band Level-2 data is partly PROVISIONAL, so values can change as the products mature.
  • Each map is one repeat-pass pair (about 12 days), not a long record. ITS_LIVE is a 2024 annual average, so the Pine Island check compares flow patterns, not the same days.
  • The Copernicus flood map is from 20 January, while the radar pair ends earlier. The Big Sur fire perimeters are coarse, so a tolerance version of the check is reported next to the strict one.
  • The Mozambique population figure (about 47,300 people) is a WorldPop modelled estimate for the mapped area, not a count of people affected.
  • These are research visualizations, not operational emergency products.

How this meets the judging criteria

  • Impact: tackles disaster mapping and trust in radar results, across four kinds of hazard and the sea-level science NISAR was built for.
  • Creativity: agreement and disagreement drawn on the map, plus 3D relief where height follows change strength, so a radar image reads without training.
  • Validity: a stated hypothesis, a fixed method, one independent or official check per event, figures read from the app's own data, caveats stated, and the weaker results (Big Sur, Hayli Gubbi) shown openly.
  • Relevance: built entirely on NISAR L-band Level-2 products from the ASF DAAC (GUNW, GCOV, GOFF), with NASA ITS_LIVE and ASF HyP3 as references, plus ISRO, ESA and ASI partner data.
  • Presentation: a 30-second video, a guided in-app flyby and a Data and methods panel tell the same story at three depths, in an app built to work as well on a mobile as on a desktop.

Part of a larger project

NISAR SAR Observatory sits next to XPLORE, a separate solar system and satellite tracker also built by Stephen Pham. XPLORE tracks 65,000+ satellites and shares the same globe and loading system.
